content: Geriatrics is a specialized field of medicine that concentrates on promoting health, preventing diseases, and managing disabilities in older adults. It is distinct from gerontology, which is the scientific study of the aging process itself. The term geriatrics originates from the Greek words geron, meaning old man, and iatros, meaning healer. This term was first introduced in 1909 by Dr. Ignatz Leo Nascher. Interestingly, it shares linguistic roots with the Sanskrit word Jara, which also means old. In the United States, geriatricians are primary care physicians who are board-certified in either family medicine or internal medicine. They undergo additional specialized training to earn the Certificate of Added Qualifications (CAQ) in geriatric medicine. In contrast, in the United Kingdom, most geriatricians work as hospital-based physicians, although some focus on community-based geriatrics. While geriatrics was initially a distinct specialty, it has been integrated into general medicine since the late 1970s. As a result, most geriatricians in the UK are accredited in both general and geriatric medicine. Specialized areas within geriatrics include orthogeriatrics, which involves collaboration with orthopedic surgeons and focuses on conditions like osteoporosis and rehabilitation. Another subspecialty is psychogeriatrics, which addresses mental health conditions common in older adults, such as dementia and depression. Rehabilitation is another critical aspect of geriatrics, often involving intermediate care. This type of care is typically provided to patients referred by hospitals or general practitioners and focuses on short-term, intensive physical therapy to restore musculoskeletal function. Rehabilitation also addresses issues such as medication mismanagement, which can lead to health deterioration and reduced independence in elderly patients. The modern practice of geriatrics in the United Kingdom owes much to Dr. Marjorie Warren, often referred to as the Mother of Geriatrics. Dr. Warren emphasized the importance of rehabilitation in the care of older adults. Her work in a London Workhouse infirmary led her to advocate for comprehensive care that included diagnosis, treatment, and support, rather than merely providing sustenance until death. She demonstrated that with proper assessment and treatment, even bedridden patients could regain some level of independence. The field of geriatrics in the UK has a strong tradition of multidisciplinary collaboration, recognizing the contributions of various healthcare professionals in optimizing the well-being and independence of older adults. Another influential figure in British geriatrics is Bernard Isaacs, who identified the giants of geriatrics: incontinence, immobility, impaired intellect, and instability. Isaacs argued that most common problems in older adults could be traced back to one of these four issues. The care of older adults in the UK has been further advanced by the implementation of the National Service Frameworks for Older People, which outlines key areas requiring attention. One of the most urgent challenges in geriatrics today is the prevention and management of delirium. Delirium is a condition characterized by confusion and disorientation, often triggered by the unfamiliar and stressful environment of a hospital stay. This condition can lead to a decline in the patient's overall health, prolong hospitalization, and result in additional complications. Effective management of delirium involves keeping the patient mentally engaged and oriented to reality, as well as providing specialized care to meet their unique needs. The Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP), developed at Yale New Haven Hospital, is a system designed to prevent delirium and improve the quality of care for elderly patients. This program has been adopted by several hospitals and has evolved into the more comprehensive Elder Horizons Program. In addition to preventing delirium, this program aims to maintain mobility and preserve functional and cognitive abilities in older adults. Pharmacological management in geriatrics is a critical area of focus due to the physiological and psychological changes that occur with aging. These changes can affect drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination, altering the efficacy and side effect profiles of many medications. For example, changes in the gastrointestinal system, body fat composition, and muscle mass can influence how drugs are processed in the body. Additionally, older adults are at higher risk for medication errors, including the use of potentially inappropriate medications and dangerous drug interactions. Another significant concern is the ability of elderly individuals, particularly those with memory loss or cognitive impairments, to adhere to prescribed medication regimens. Studies have shown that a substantial proportion of older adults struggle with medication compliance. For instance, one study found that 25% of participants admitted to skipping doses or halving them, while one-third reported noncompliance with their medication schedules.
